## Encoding

### `to-base64`

**To Base64**: Encodes raw bytes as Base64 text. e.g. "hello" becomes "aGVsbG8=".

- Aliases: b64, base64 encode
- Inverse: [`from-base64`](#from-base64)
- More info: <https://wikipedia.org/wiki/Base64>
- Output: text

Arguments:

- `padding` (CLI: `--no-padding`, template: `padding`): Padding (=). Default: `true`.

Examples:

```sh
ops to-base64 hello  # -> "aGVsbG8="
ops to-base64 --no-padding hello  # -> "aGVsbG8"
```

### `from-base64`

**From Base64**: Decodes Base64 text into raw bytes. e.g. "aGVsbG8=" becomes "hello".

- Aliases: b64, base64 decode
- Inverse: [`to-base64`](#to-base64)
- More info: <https://wikipedia.org/wiki/Base64>
- Output: binary (may contain arbitrary bytes)

Arguments:

- `strict` (CLI: `--strict`, template: `strict`): Strict mode. Fail on non-alphabet characters and invalid padding instead of ignoring them. Default: `false`.

Examples:

```sh
ops from-base64 aGVsbG8=  # -> "hello"
ops from-base64 $'aGVs\nbG8'  # -> "hello"
```

### `to-base64url`

**To Base64url**: Encodes raw bytes as URL-safe Base64 (- and _ instead of + and /), without padding by default. e.g. "ÿÿ" becomes "w7_Dvw".

- Aliases: b64url, base64url encode
- Inverse: [`from-base64url`](#from-base64url)
- More info: <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4648#section-5>
- Output: text

Arguments:

- `padding` (CLI: `--padding`, template: `padding`): Padding (=). Default: `false`.

Examples:

```sh
ops to-base64url 'ÿÿ'  # -> "w7_Dvw"
ops to-base64url --padding 'ÿÿ'  # -> "w7_Dvw=="
```

### `from-base64url`

**From Base64url**: Decodes URL-safe Base64 (- and _ instead of + and /) into raw bytes. e.g. "w7_Dvw" becomes "ÿÿ".

- Aliases: b64url, base64url decode, jwt
- Inverse: [`to-base64url`](#to-base64url)
- More info: <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4648#section-5>
- Output: binary (may contain arbitrary bytes)

Arguments:

- `strict` (CLI: `--strict`, template: `strict`): Strict mode. Fail on non-alphabet characters and invalid padding instead of ignoring them. Default: `false`.

Examples:

```sh
ops from-base64url w7_Dvw  # -> "ÿÿ"
ops from-base64url w7_Dvw==  # -> "ÿÿ"
```

### `to-base32`

**To Base32**: Encodes raw bytes as Base32 text. e.g. "hello" becomes "NBSWY3DP".

- Aliases: b32, base32 encode
- Inverse: [`from-base32`](#from-base32)
- More info: <https://wikipedia.org/wiki/Base32>
- Output: text

Arguments:

- `alphabet` (CLI: `--alphabet`, template: `alphabet`): Alphabet. One of `base32` (Standard (RFC 4648): A-Z2-7=), `base32hex` (Extended hex (RFC 4648 §7): 0-9A-V=). Default: `base32`.
- `padding` (CLI: `--no-padding`, template: `padding`): Padding (=). Default: `true`.

Examples:

```sh
ops to-base32 hello  # -> "NBSWY3DP"
ops to-base32 hi  # -> "NBUQ===="
ops to-base32 --alphabet base32hex --no-padding hi  # -> "D1KG"
```

### `from-base32`

**From Base32**: Decodes Base32 text into raw bytes, ignoring case, whitespace and padding. e.g. "NBSWY3DP" becomes "hello".

- Aliases: b32, base32 decode
- Inverse: [`to-base32`](#to-base32)
- More info: <https://wikipedia.org/wiki/Base32>
- Output: binary (may contain arbitrary bytes)

Arguments:

- `alphabet` (CLI: `--alphabet`, template: `alphabet`): Alphabet. One of `base32` (Standard (RFC 4648): A-Z2-7=), `base32hex` (Extended hex (RFC 4648 §7): 0-9A-V=). Default: `base32`.

Examples:

```sh
ops from-base32 NBSWY3DP  # -> "hello"
ops from-base32 nbuq====  # -> "hi"
ops from-base32 --alphabet base32hex D1KG  # -> "hi"
```

### `to-base58`

**To Base58**: Encodes raw bytes as Base58 text, as used by Bitcoin addresses. Leading zero bytes become "1". e.g. "hello" becomes "Cn8eVZg".

- Aliases: b58, base58 encode, bitcoin
- Inverse: [`from-base58`](#from-base58)
- More info: <https://wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary-to-text_encoding#Base58>
- Output: text

Arguments:

- `alphabet` (CLI: `--alphabet`, template: `alphabet`): Alphabet. One of `bitcoin` (Bitcoin: 1-9A-HJ-NP-Za-km-z), `flickr` (Flickr: 1-9a-km-zA-HJ-NP-Z), `ripple` (Ripple: rpshnaf39wBUDNEGHJKLM4PQRST7VWXYZ2bcdeCg65jkm8oFqi1tuvAxyz). Default: `bitcoin`.

Examples:

```sh
ops to-base58 hello  # -> "Cn8eVZg"
ops to-base58 'Hello World!'  # -> "2NEpo7TZRRrLZSi2U"
```

### `from-base58`

**From Base58**: Decodes Base58 text into raw bytes, ignoring whitespace. e.g. "Cn8eVZg" becomes "hello".

- Aliases: b58, base58 decode, bitcoin
- Inverse: [`to-base58`](#to-base58)
- More info: <https://wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary-to-text_encoding#Base58>
- Output: binary (may contain arbitrary bytes)

Arguments:

- `alphabet` (CLI: `--alphabet`, template: `alphabet`): Alphabet. One of `bitcoin` (Bitcoin: 1-9A-HJ-NP-Za-km-z), `flickr` (Flickr: 1-9a-km-zA-HJ-NP-Z), `ripple` (Ripple: rpshnaf39wBUDNEGHJKLM4PQRST7VWXYZ2bcdeCg65jkm8oFqi1tuvAxyz). Default: `bitcoin`.

Examples:

```sh
ops from-base58 Cn8eVZg  # -> "hello"
ops from-base58 2NEpo7TZRRrLZSi2U  # -> "Hello World!"
```

### `to-base62`

**To Base62**: Encodes raw bytes as Base62 text (letters and digits only). Leading zero bytes become "0". e.g. "hello" becomes "7tQLFHz".

- Aliases: b62, base62 encode
- Inverse: [`from-base62`](#from-base62)
- More info: <https://wikipedia.org/wiki/Base62>
- Output: text

Arguments:

- `alphabet` (CLI: `--alphabet`, template: `alphabet`): Alphabet. One of `0-9A-Za-z` (Digits, uppercase, lowercase (GMP)), `0-9a-zA-Z` (Digits, lowercase, uppercase). Default: `0-9A-Za-z`.

Examples:

```sh
ops to-base62 hello  # -> "7tQLFHz"
ops to-base62 --alphabet 0-9a-zA-Z hello  # -> "7TqlfhZ"
```

### `from-base62`

**From Base62**: Decodes Base62 text into raw bytes, ignoring whitespace. e.g. "7tQLFHz" becomes "hello".

- Aliases: b62, base62 decode
- Inverse: [`to-base62`](#to-base62)
- More info: <https://wikipedia.org/wiki/Base62>
- Output: binary (may contain arbitrary bytes)

Arguments:

- `alphabet` (CLI: `--alphabet`, template: `alphabet`): Alphabet. One of `0-9A-Za-z` (Digits, uppercase, lowercase (GMP)), `0-9a-zA-Z` (Digits, lowercase, uppercase). Default: `0-9A-Za-z`.

Examples:

```sh
ops from-base62 7tQLFHz  # -> "hello"
ops from-base62 --alphabet 0-9a-zA-Z 7TqlfhZ  # -> "hello"
```

### `to-hex`

**To Hex**: Encodes raw bytes as hexadecimal text. e.g. "hello" becomes "68656c6c6f".

- Aliases: hex encode, base16, xxd
- Inverse: [`from-hex`](#from-hex)
- More info: <https://wikipedia.org/wiki/Hexadecimal>
- Output: text

Arguments:

- `delimiter` (CLI: `--delimiter`, template: `delimiter`): Delimiter. One of `none` (None: 68656c6c6f), `space` (Space: 68 65 6c 6c 6f), `colon` (Colon: 68:65:6c:6c:6f), `comma` (Comma: 68,65,6c,6c,6f), `escape` (Escape sequences: \x68\x65\x6c\x6c\x6f), `0x` (C array: 0x68, 0x65, 0x6c, 0x6c, 0x6f). Default: `none`.
- `uppercase` (CLI: `--uppercase`, template: `uppercase`): Uppercase. Default: `false`.

Examples:

```sh
ops to-hex hello  # -> "68656c6c6f"
ops to-hex --delimiter colon --uppercase hello  # -> "68:65:6C:6C:6F"
ops to-hex --delimiter escape hi  # -> "\\x68\\x69"
```

### `from-hex`

**From Hex**: Decodes hexadecimal text into raw bytes, ignoring case, whitespace, separators (: , ; . % -) and 0x or \x prefixes. e.g. "68656c6c6f" becomes "hello".

- Aliases: hex decode, base16, unhex, xxd -r
- Inverse: [`to-hex`](#to-hex)
- More info: <https://wikipedia.org/wiki/Hexadecimal>
- Output: binary (may contain arbitrary bytes)

No arguments.

Examples:

```sh
ops from-hex 68656c6c6f  # -> "hello"
ops from-hex 68:65:6C:6C:6F  # -> "hello"
ops from-hex '0x68, 0x69'  # -> "hi"
ops from-hex '\x68\x69'  # -> "hi"
```

### `url-encode`

**URL Encode**: Encodes bytes as %XX sequences (percent-encoding). e.g. "a b" becomes "a%20b".

- Aliases: percent encode, urlencode
- Inverse: [`url-decode`](#url-decode)
- More info: <https://wikipedia.org/wiki/Percent-encoding>
- Output: text

Arguments:

- `encodeAll` (CLI: `--encode-all`, template: `encode-all`): Encode all special chars. Also encode reserved characters such as / ? & = (like encodeURIComponent). Default: `false`.

Examples:

```sh
ops url-encode 'a b&c=é'  # -> "a%20b&c=%C3%A9"
ops url-encode --encode-all 'a b&c=é'  # -> "a%20b%26c%3D%C3%A9"
```

### `url-decode`

**URL Decode**: Decodes %XX sequences (percent-encoding) into bytes. Invalid sequences are left as is.

- Aliases: percent decode, urldecode
- Inverse: [`url-encode`](#url-encode)
- More info: <https://wikipedia.org/wiki/Percent-encoding>
- Output: binary (may contain arbitrary bytes)

Arguments:

- `plusAsSpace` (CLI: `--no-plus-as-space`, template: `plus-as-space`): Treat "+" as space. HTML form behavior (application/x-www-form-urlencoded). Default: `true`.

Examples:

```sh
ops url-decode a%20b%26c%3D%C3%A9  # -> "a b&c=é"
ops url-decode a+b  # -> "a b"
ops url-decode --no-plus-as-space a+b  # -> "a+b"
```

### `html-encode`

**HTML Encode**: Escapes & < > " and ' as HTML entities. e.g. "<b>" becomes "&lt;b&gt;".

- Aliases: html escape, html entities
- Inverse: [`html-decode`](#html-decode)
- More info: <https://wikipedia.org/wiki/Character_encodings_in_HTML>
- Output: binary (may contain arbitrary bytes)

Arguments:

- `encodeNonAscii` (CLI: `--encode-non-ascii`, template: `encode-non-ascii`): Encode non-ASCII characters. Also write characters outside ASCII as numeric entities, e.g. é as &#233;. Default: `false`.

Examples:

```sh
ops html-encode '<a href="x">Tom & Jerry</a>'  # -> "&lt;a href=&quot;x&quot;&gt;Tom &amp; Jerry&lt;/a&gt;"
ops html-encode --encode-non-ascii 'café €'  # -> "caf&#233; &#8364;"
```

### `html-decode`

**HTML Decode**: Decodes HTML entities: numeric (&#233; &#xE9;) and named HTML 4 ones (&eacute; &amp; ...). Unknown entities are left as is. e.g. "&lt;b&gt;" becomes "<b>".

- Aliases: html unescape, html entities
- Inverse: [`html-encode`](#html-encode)
- More info: <https://wikipedia.org/wiki/Character_encodings_in_HTML>
- Output: binary (may contain arbitrary bytes)

No arguments.

Examples:

```sh
ops html-decode '&lt;a href=&quot;x&quot;&gt;Tom &amp; Jerry&lt;/a&gt;'  # -> "<a href=\"x\">Tom & Jerry</a>"
ops html-decode 'caf&eacute; &#8364; &#x263A; &unknown;'  # -> "café € ☺ &unknown;"
```


### `bcrypt`

**Bcrypt**: Hashes the input (a password) with bcrypt, using a random salt unless one is given. Only the first 72 bytes are used.

- Aliases: password hash, blowfish
- More info: <https://wikipedia.org/wiki/Bcrypt>
- Output: text

Arguments:

- `rounds` (CLI: `--rounds`, template: `rounds`): Cost. Log2 of the number of rounds: each step doubles the computing time. Number (min 4, max 31). Default: `10`.
- `salt` (CLI: `--salt`, template: `salt`): Salt. 22 characters from ./A-Za-z0-9. Leave empty for a random salt. Default: ``.

Examples:

```sh
ops bcrypt --rounds 4 --salt abcdefghijklmnopqrstuu hello  # -> "$2b$04$abcdefghijklmnopqrstuuwHJMEGjfAzmL1lWmUmlphguIbWfjYey"
```

## Data format

### `json-format`

**JSON format**: Pretty-prints or minifies JSON. Numbers are kept digit for digit, and keys in their original order.

- Aliases: json beautify, json prettify, json minify, jq
- More info: <https://www.json.org>
- Output: binary (may contain arbitrary bytes)

Arguments:

- `indent` (CLI: `--indent`, template: `indent`): Indentation. One of `2` (2 spaces), `4` (4 spaces), `tab` (Tab), `minify` (None, on a single line). Default: `2`.

Examples:

```sh
ops json-format '{"a":1,"b":[true,null],"c":{}}'  # -> "{\n  \"a\": 1,\n  \"b\": [\n    true,\n    null\n  ],\n  \"c\": {}\n}"
ops json-format --indent minify $'{ "id": 12345678901234567890,\n  "tags": [ "x" ] }'  # -> "{\"id\":12345678901234567890,\"tags\":[\"x\"]}"
```

### `json-to-yaml`

**JSON to YAML**: Converts JSON to YAML. Strings that some YAML parsers would read as another type, such as "yes", are quoted.

- Aliases: yaml
- Inverse: [`yaml-to-json`](#yaml-to-json)
- More info: <https://yaml.org>
- Output: binary (may contain arbitrary bytes)

No arguments.

Examples:

```sh
ops json-to-yaml '{"name":"ops","tags":["a","b"],"count":1}'  # -> "name: ops\ntags:\n  - a\n  - b\ncount: 1\n"
ops json-to-yaml '{"enabled":"yes"}'  # -> "enabled: \"yes\"\n"
```

### `yaml-to-json`

**YAML to JSON**: Converts a YAML document to JSON.

- Aliases: yml, yaml
- Inverse: [`json-to-yaml`](#json-to-yaml)
- More info: <https://yaml.org>
- Output: binary (may contain arbitrary bytes)

Arguments:

- `indent` (CLI: `--indent`, template: `indent`): Indentation. One of `2` (2 spaces), `4` (4 spaces), `tab` (Tab), `minify` (None, on a single line). Default: `2`.

Examples:

```sh
ops yaml-to-json --indent minify $'name: ops\ntags: [a, b]\nn: 1\n'  # -> "{\"name\":\"ops\",\"tags\":[\"a\",\"b\"],\"n\":1}"
ops yaml-to-json $'a:\n  - true\n  - ~\n'  # -> "{\n  \"a\": [\n    true,\n    null\n  ]\n}"
```

### `hex-to-rgb`

**Hex to RGB**: Converts hex colors (one per line) to RGB. e.g. "#ff8800" becomes "rgb(255, 136, 0)".

- Aliases: color, colour, css color
- More info: <https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/CSS/hex-color>
- Output: binary (may contain arbitrary bytes)

Arguments:

- `format` (CLI: `--format`, template: `format`): Format. One of `css` (CSS: rgb(255, 136, 0) or rgba(255, 136, 0, 0.5)), `values` (Values: 255, 136, 0). Default: `css`.

Examples:

```sh
ops hex-to-rgb '#ff8800'  # -> "rgb(255, 136, 0)"
ops hex-to-rgb $'#f80\n#FF880080'  # -> "rgb(255, 136, 0)\nrgba(255, 136, 0, 0.502)"
ops hex-to-rgb --format values ff8800  # -> "255, 136, 0"
```

## Text

### `to-lower-case`

**To lower case**: Converts the text to lowercase. e.g. "HÉLLO" becomes "héllo".

- Aliases: lowercase
- Output: binary (may contain arbitrary bytes)

No arguments.

Examples:

```sh
ops to-lower-case 'HÉLLO World'  # -> "héllo world"
```

### `to-upper-case`

**To UPPER CASE**: Converts the text to uppercase. e.g. "héllo" becomes "HÉLLO".

- Aliases: uppercase, capitals
- Output: binary (may contain arbitrary bytes)

No arguments.

Examples:

```sh
ops to-upper-case 'héllo world'  # -> "HÉLLO WORLD"
```

### `to-title-case`

**To Title Case**: Capitalizes the first letter of every word and lowercases the others. e.g. "hello WORLD" becomes "Hello World".

- Aliases: capitalize, titlecase
- Output: binary (may contain arbitrary bytes)

No arguments.

Examples:

```sh
ops to-title-case 'hello WORLD, don'\''t panic'  # -> "Hello World, Don't Panic"
```

### `to-camel-case`

**To camelCase**: Joins the words with the first one in lowercase and the others capitalized. e.g. "hello world" becomes "helloWorld". Each line is converted separately.

- Aliases: camelcase, lower camel case
- Output: binary (may contain arbitrary bytes)

No arguments.

Examples:

```sh
ops to-camel-case $'Hello big_world\nXMLHttpRequest'  # -> "helloBigWorld\nxmlHttpRequest"
```

### `to-pascal-case`

**To PascalCase**: Joins the capitalized words. e.g. "hello world" becomes "HelloWorld". Each line is converted separately.

- Aliases: pascalcase, upper camel case
- Output: binary (may contain arbitrary bytes)

No arguments.

Examples:

```sh
ops to-pascal-case 'hello big_world'  # -> "HelloBigWorld"
```

### `to-snake-case`

**To snake_case**: Joins the lowercase words with underscores. e.g. "helloWorld" becomes "hello_world". Each line is converted separately.

- Aliases: snakecase, underscore
- Output: binary (may contain arbitrary bytes)

No arguments.

Examples:

```sh
ops to-snake-case 'Hello bigWorld'  # -> "hello_big_world"
```

### `to-kebab-case`

**To kebab-case**: Joins the lowercase words with hyphens. e.g. "helloWorld" becomes "hello-world". Each line is converted separately.

- Aliases: kebabcase, dash case, hyphen
- Output: binary (may contain arbitrary bytes)

No arguments.

Examples:

```sh
ops to-kebab-case 'Hello bigWorld'  # -> "hello-big-world"
```

### `to-slug`

**To slug**: Makes a URL-friendly slug: removes accents, lowercases, and replaces everything but letters and digits with a separator. e.g. "Héllo, World!" becomes "hello-world". Each line is converted separately.

- Aliases: slugify, permalink
- Output: binary (may contain arbitrary bytes)

Arguments:

- `separator` (CLI: `--separator`, template: `separator`): Separator. Default: `-`.

Examples:

```sh
ops to-slug 'Héllo, World!'  # -> "hello-world"
ops to-slug --separator _ 'Straße & Œuvre'  # -> "strasse_oeuvre"
```

### `sort-lines`

**Sort lines**: Sorts the lines by Unicode code point, like `LC_ALL=C sort`, or in natural order.

- Aliases: sort, order
- Output: binary (may contain arbitrary bytes)

Arguments:

- `reverse` (CLI: `--reverse`, template: `reverse`): Reverse. Sort in descending order. Default: `false`.
- `ignoreCase` (CLI: `--ignore-case`, template: `ignore-case`): Ignore case. Default: `false`.
- `natural` (CLI: `--natural`, template: `natural`): Natural order. Compare numbers by value ("2" before "10") and letters alphabetically ("a" before "B"). Default: `false`.

Examples:

```sh
ops sort-lines $'b\nB\na\n10\n2'  # -> "10\n2\nB\na\nb"
ops sort-lines --natural --ignore-case $'b\nB\na\n10\n2'  # -> "2\n10\na\nb\nB"
ops sort-lines --reverse $'a\nc\nb'  # -> "c\nb\na"
```

### `shuffle-lines`

**Shuffle lines**: Puts the lines in a random order.

- Aliases: shuf, randomize
- Output: binary (may contain arbitrary bytes)

Arguments:

- `seed` (CLI: `--seed`, template: `seed`): Seed. Gives the same order every time for the same seed and input. Leave empty for a random order. Default: ``.

Examples:

```sh
ops shuffle-lines --seed 42 $'a\nb\nc\nd'  # -> "c\na\nd\nb"
```

### `unique-lines`

**Unique lines**: Removes duplicate lines, keeping the first occurrence of each, even when duplicates are not adjacent.

- Aliases: uniq, dedupe, remove duplicates
- Output: binary (may contain arbitrary bytes)

Arguments:

- `ignoreCase` (CLI: `--ignore-case`, template: `ignore-case`): Ignore case. Default: `false`.

Examples:

```sh
ops unique-lines $'a\nb\na\nc\nb'  # -> "a\nb\nc"
ops unique-lines --ignore-case $'a\nA\nb'  # -> "a\nb"
```

### `reverse-lines`

**Reverse lines**: Reverses the order of the lines, like `tac`.

- Aliases: tac
- Output: binary (may contain arbitrary bytes)

No arguments.

Examples:

```sh
ops reverse-lines $'a\nb\nc\n'  # -> "c\nb\na\n"
```

### `add-line-numbers`

**Add line numbers**: Prefixes every line with its number, right-aligned, like `cat -n`.

- Aliases: line numberer, nl, cat -n
- Output: binary (may contain arbitrary bytes)

Arguments:

- `start` (CLI: `--start`, template: `start`): First number. Number. Default: `1`.
- `separator` (CLI: `--separator`, template: `separator`): Separator. Placed between the number and the line. Default: ` `.

Examples:

```sh
ops add-line-numbers $'a\nb'  # -> "1 a\n2 b"
ops add-line-numbers --start 9 --separator ': ' $'a\nb\nc'  # -> " 9: a\n10: b\n11: c"
```

### `reverse-text`

**Reverse text**: Reverses the order of the characters. Accented letters and emoji stay intact. e.g. "héllo" becomes "olléh".

- Aliases: reverse string, mirror
- Output: binary (may contain arbitrary bytes)

No arguments.

Examples:

```sh
ops reverse-text 'héllo'  # -> "olléh"
ops reverse-text 'a👍🏽b'  # -> "b👍🏽a"
```

### `remove-newlines`

**Remove newlines**: Removes every line break (LF, CRLF and CR), or replaces it with the given text.

- Aliases: join lines, single line, strip newlines
- Output: binary (may contain arbitrary bytes)

Arguments:

- `replacement` (CLI: `--replacement`, template: `replacement`): Replacement. Default: ``.

Examples:

```sh
ops remove-newlines $'a\nb\x0d\nc'  # -> "abc"
ops remove-newlines --replacement ', ' $'a\nb\nc'  # -> "a, b, c"
```

### `remove-whitespace`

**Remove whitespace**: Removes all spaces, tabs, line breaks and other Unicode whitespace.

- Aliases: remove spaces, strip whitespace, trim
- Output: binary (may contain arbitrary bytes)

Arguments:

- `keepNewlines` (CLI: `--keep-newlines`, template: `keep-newlines`): Keep line breaks. Default: `false`.

Examples:

```sh
ops remove-whitespace $'a b\tc\nd'  # -> "abcd"
ops remove-whitespace --keep-newlines $'a b\nc d'  # -> "ab\ncd"
```

### `escape-quotes`

**Escape quotes**: Puts a backslash before quotes, and before backslashes so the result is unambiguous. e.g. say "hi" becomes say \"hi\".

- Aliases: escape string, addslashes
- Output: binary (may contain arbitrary bytes)

Arguments:

- `quotes` (CLI: `--quotes`, template: `quotes`): Quotes. One of `double` (Double quotes (")), `single` (Single quotes (')), `both` (Both). Default: `double`.
- `escapeBackslashes` (CLI: `--no-escape-backslashes`, template: `escape-backslashes`): Escape backslashes. Default: `true`.

Examples:

```sh
ops escape-quotes 'say "hi" \o/'  # -> "say \\\"hi\\\" \\\\o/"
ops escape-quotes --quotes single 'it'\''s "ok"'  # -> "it\\'s \"ok\""
ops escape-quotes --quotes both --no-escape-backslashes ''\''a'\'' "b" \'  # -> "\\'a\\' \\\"b\\\" \\"
```

### `count-chars`

**Count characters**: Counts the characters of the input, line breaks included, like `wc -m`.

- Aliases: length, wc -m, char count
- Output: text

Arguments:

- `unit` (CLI: `--unit`, template: `unit`): Unit. One of `graphemes` (Characters as displayed (é and 👍🏽 count as 1)), `codepoints` (Unicode code points), `bytes` (Bytes). Default: `graphemes`.

Examples:

```sh
ops count-chars 'héllo 👍🏽'  # -> "7"
ops count-chars --unit codepoints 'héllo 👍🏽'  # -> "8"
ops count-chars --unit bytes 'héllo 👍🏽'  # -> "15"
```

### `count-lines`

**Count lines**: Counts the lines of the input. Unlike `wc -l`, a last line without a line break is counted.

- Aliases: wc -l, line count
- Output: text

No arguments.

Examples:

```sh
ops count-lines $'a\nb\nc'  # -> "3"
ops count-lines $'a\nb\n'  # -> "2"
ops count-lines ''  # -> "0"
```

### `count-words`

**Count words**: Counts the words of the input, separated by whitespace, like `wc -w`.

- Aliases: wc -w, word count
- Output: text

No arguments.

Examples:

```sh
ops count-words $'  hello big\n world '  # -> "3"
```

## Extractors

### `extract-ips`

**Extract IP addresses**: Lists the IPv4 and IPv6 addresses found in the text, one per line.

- Aliases: ipv4, ipv6, find ip, grep ip
- Output: binary (may contain arbitrary bytes)

Arguments:

- `version` (CLI: `--version`, template: `version`): Version. One of `both` (IPv4 and IPv6), `ipv4` (IPv4 only), `ipv6` (IPv6 only). Default: `both`.
- `unique` (CLI: `--unique`, template: `unique`): Unique. Only list each value once. Default: `false`.
- `sort` (CLI: `--sort`, template: `sort`): Sort. Default: `false`.

Examples:

```sh
ops extract-ips 'from 10.0.0.1 to 2001:db8::1, not 1.2.3.4.5 or 256.1.1.1'  # -> "10.0.0.1\n2001:db8::1"
ops extract-ips --version ipv4 '::1 ::ffff:192.168.1.1 8.8.8.8'  # -> "8.8.8.8"
```

### `extract-emails`

**Extract email addresses**: Lists the email addresses found in the text, one per line.

- Aliases: find email, grep email
- Output: binary (may contain arbitrary bytes)

Arguments:

- `unique` (CLI: `--unique`, template: `unique`): Unique. Only list each value once. Default: `false`.
- `sort` (CLI: `--sort`, template: `sort`): Sort. Default: `false`.

Examples:

```sh
ops extract-emails 'Contact: <john.doe@example.com>, jane+tag@mail.example.org.'  # -> "john.doe@example.com\njane+tag@mail.example.org"
ops extract-emails --unique --sort 'b@x.io a@x.io b@x.io'  # -> "a@x.io\nb@x.io"
```

### `extract-urls`

**Extract URLs**: Lists the URLs (anything like scheme://...) found in the text, one per line.

- Aliases: find url, grep url, links
- Output: binary (may contain arbitrary bytes)

Arguments:

- `unique` (CLI: `--unique`, template: `unique`): Unique. Only list each value once. Default: `false`.
- `sort` (CLI: `--sort`, template: `sort`): Sort. Default: `false`.

Examples:

```sh
ops extract-urls 'See https://example.com/a?b=1, (or http://wiki.org/A_(b)) and ftp://x.org/file.'  # -> "https://example.com/a?b=1\nhttp://wiki.org/A_(b)\nftp://x.org/file"
```
